lesson.title: Eat or Be Eaten: The Dynamics of Predator and Prey
lesson.summary: Predation, in which one organism captures, kills, and consumes another for food, is a plus-minus interspecific interaction that drives coevolution between predators and prey and can produce linked, cyclical population dynamics between them.
lesson.body:
Predation is one of the most immediately intuitive interspecific interactions: a predator captures, kills, and consumes another organism, its prey, for nutrition. In the plus-minus framework from the previous chapter, the predator clearly gains, while the individual prey animal clearly loses, in the most direct way possible. But predation's effects extend well beyond any single meal, shaping how both predator and prey species evolve over generations, and in some cases driving recognizable long-term patterns in both populations' numbers.

Because predation exerts strong, ongoing selective pressure, it tends to drive an evolutionary back and forth between predator and prey, sometimes called a coevolutionary arms race. Predators evolve traits that improve their ability to detect, chase down, or subdue prey: keen eyesight or smell, speed, sharp claws and teeth, venom, or coordinated group hunting. Prey species, in turn, evolve traits that improve their odds of avoiding capture: camouflage that helps them blend into their surroundings, warning coloration paired with genuine toxicity that discourages predators from attacking at all, mimicry of a more dangerous or unpalatable species, alarm calls that warn others in a group, herding or flocking behavior that offers safety in numbers, and fast escape reflexes. Neither side achieves a permanent advantage, since any improvement on one side tends to favor a counter-adaptation on the other over evolutionary time.

One of the most famous real examples of predator-prey population dynamics comes from Canada, where the snowshoe hare and its main predator, the Canada lynx, have been tracked for roughly a century using historical fur trapping records. These records reveal a recurring cyclical pattern, hare numbers rise, then lynx numbers rise not long afterward as they benefit from abundant prey, then hare numbers fall as heavier predation combined with other pressures takes its toll, followed by a decline in lynx numbers as their food supply shrinks, after which the cycle begins again. This case is genuinely one of the best documented long-term wildlife datasets in ecology, but it is worth being careful not to oversimplify it: later research has shown that the hare-lynx cycle is not driven by predation alone. Fluctuations in the hares' plant food supply, including changes in the chemical defenses those plants produce under heavy browsing, and pressure from other predators besides lynx, all appear to contribute to the pattern as well. The lesson is less that predators alone control prey numbers in a simple back and forth, and more that predator-prey dynamics are typically embedded in a wider web of interacting factors, even in the clearest textbook cases.

Mathematical models, most notably the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey equations, formalize the basic logic of how predator and prey numbers can rise and fall in a linked, cyclical way, though like the logistic growth model discussed earlier, these are simplified representations rather than exact descriptions of any particular real population.

Predation also connects directly back to density-dependent regulation from earlier in this unit: as a prey population becomes denser, it often becomes an easier or more attractive target for predators, meaning predation pressure on that population can intensify with density, one of the several density-dependent mechanisms that tend to pull a growing population back toward its carrying capacity.
